cards.statement: Administrators verify a custom domain before using it in a new Microsoft Entra ID user's UPN.
cards.explanation: Microsoft Entra ID checks a new user's UPN domain against the tenant's verified domains. Verification enables the administrator to use the custom suffix.

source.title: Create User

cards.statement: Administrators edit the department of a user managed by Windows Server Active Directory in Microsoft Entra ID.
cards.explanation: For a user managed by Windows Server Active Directory, administrators update the department there. Synchronization carries the change to Microsoft Entra ID.
cards.misconception: Synced job information is editable in the cloud while Windows Server Active Directory remains authoritative.

source.title: Manage user profile information in the Microsoft Entra admin center

cards.statement: Administrators can add device objects as members of Microsoft Entra ID security groups.
cards.explanation: Security groups accept users, devices and service principals as members, while Microsoft 365 groups accept only users, so device targeting relies on security groups.

source.title: Learn About Groups, Group Membership, and Access - Microsoft Entra

cards.statement: Administrators can manually add a user to a Microsoft Entra ID group with dynamic membership.
cards.explanation: Microsoft Entra ID determines dynamic membership from the group's rule. Administrators change the rule or the relevant user attributes to change membership.
cards.misconception: Dynamic membership permits manual exceptions.

source.title: Manage rules for dynamic membership groups in Microsoft Entra ID

cards.statement: Group-based licensing reaches users through groups nested inside the licensed Microsoft Entra ID group.
cards.explanation: Group-based licensing processes the licensed group's direct user members. Users reached through a nested group do not receive that license assignment.
cards.misconception: Licenses assigned to a parent group reach users through nested groups.

source.title: Assign or unassign licenses to a group in the Microsoft 365 admin center

cards.statement: Group-based licensing uses the tenant's location when a user's usage location is unset.
cards.explanation: Group-based licensing falls back to the tenant's location for a user whose location is unset. Set individual usage locations when users work in different locations.

source.title: Assign or unassign licenses to a group in the Microsoft 365 admin center

cards.statement: Microsoft Entra External ID lets B2B guests invite external users under the default invitation settings.
cards.explanation: The default invitation policy includes B2B guests. Administrators should review who is allowed to invite partners when configuring external access.
cards.volatilityNote: The default external-user invitation policy may change.

source.title: What is Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration?

cards.statement: Administrators configure trust in a partner tenant's MFA claims through external collaboration settings.
cards.explanation: Cross-tenant access settings let a tenant trust a partner tenant's MFA claims. Administrators configure that trust for the partner organization.
cards.misconception: External collaboration settings control trust in partner authentication claims.

source.title: What is Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration?

cards.statement: Administrators can enable Microsoft Entra ID self-service password reset for a selected group of users.
cards.explanation: Selecting a user group limits end-user SSPR enablement to its membership. Administrators can use this scope to pilot password reset before broad rollout.

source.title: Enable Microsoft Entra self-service password reset

cards.statement: A Reader assignment lets its holder retrieve a storage account's access keys through Azure Resource Manager.
cards.explanation: Reader exposes control-plane information but excludes the action that lists storage account keys.
cards.misconception: Reading resource information includes retrieving access keys.

source.title: Choose how to authorize access to blob data in the Azure portal

cards.statement: A subscription-level Contributor assignment covers virtual machines added to its resource groups.
cards.explanation: Resources inherit role permissions from parent scopes, including resources created after the assignment.

source.title: Understand scope for Azure RBAC

cards.statement: A resource-group Reader assignment replaces that user's subscription-level Contributor permissions.
cards.explanation: Azure RBAC combines applicable role grants. Adding Reader at a child scope leaves the broader Contributor grant effective.
cards.misconception: The most specific role assignment overrides broader grants.

source.title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

cards.statement: An administrator can remove a subscription's inherited role assignment at a child resource group.
cards.explanation: Remove an inherited role assignment at the scope where it was created; a child scope does not own that assignment.
cards.misconception: A child scope can remove the role assignment it inherits.

source.title: Remove Azure role assignments

cards.statement: A Global Administrator gains permission to manage Azure virtual machines by default.
cards.explanation: Global Administrator governs Microsoft Entra resources. Azure resource access requires an Azure role assignment or access elevation.
cards.misconception: A tenant administrator automatically manages Azure resources.

source.title: Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles

cards.statement: An Owner restricts the roles a Role Based Access Control Administrator assigns with assignment conditions.
cards.explanation: Conditions on the delegate's role assignment can restrict the roles that the delegate creates or removes.

source.title: Delegate Azure access management to others

cards.statement: An unconstrained User Access Administrator can assign themselves Owner at their assigned scope.
cards.explanation: User Access Administrator includes role-assignment permissions, which permit granting Owner to the role holder.

source.title: Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles

cards.statement: Azure keeps a service principal's role assignments after an administrator deletes that principal.
cards.explanation: Deleting the Microsoft Entra principal leaves its Azure role assignments in place; administrators should clean them up.

source.title: Understand Azure role assignments

cards.statement: An Owner assignment overrides an applicable deny assignment for the same Azure resource action.
cards.explanation: An applicable deny assignment blocks the action even when an Azure role grants it.
cards.misconception: Owner bypasses Azure deny assignments.

source.title: List Azure deny assignments

cards.statement: Azure Policy requires an authorized managed identity to remediate existing resources with the modify effect.
cards.explanation: A modify remediation task uses the identity associated with the policy assignment to make authorized resource changes.

source.title: Remediate non-compliant resources

cards.statement: Azure Policy evaluates deny before modify for a resource creation request in Resource Manager mode.
cards.explanation: In Resource Manager mode, Azure Policy evaluates modify before deny. A change to the request can affect whether the deny rule matches.
cards.misconception: Azure Policy checks denial before changing the incoming request.

source.title: Azure Policy definitions effect basics

cards.statement: Azure blocks deletion of a resource group when a resource inside it has a Delete lock.
cards.explanation: A Delete lock on a contained resource stops the entire resource-group deletion operation.

source.title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure

cards.statement: Azure rejects a VM restart when a Read-only lock applies to the VM's resource group.
cards.explanation: Restarting a VM is a control-plane action that a Read-only lock blocks, even for an otherwise authorized administrator.

source.title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure

cards.statement: Azure automatically copies a resource group's tags onto resources added to that group.
cards.explanation: Resource-group tags do not propagate automatically. Apply resource tags explicitly or configure tag inheritance through Azure Policy.
cards.misconception: Resource tags inherit from the containing resource group.

source.title: Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy

cards.statement: A resource group's location requires an administrator to place its VMs in the same Azure region.
cards.explanation: The resource-group location determines where Azure stores its metadata. Its resources can occupy different regions.
cards.misconception: Resource-group location constrains resource placement.

source.title: Manage Azure resource groups by using the Azure portal

cards.statement: Azure preserves role assignments when an administrator transfers a subscription to another Microsoft Entra tenant.
cards.explanation: A directory transfer deletes the subscription's Azure role assignments. Recreate assignments for principals in the target tenant.
cards.misconception: Azure role assignments move with a subscription across tenants.

source.title: Transfer an Azure subscription to a different Microsoft Entra directory

cards.statement: A Microsoft Cost Management budget stops Azure resources when their spending exceeds the budget amount.
cards.explanation: A budget triggers configured notifications; crossing its threshold leaves resources running and consumption continuing.
cards.misconception: A budget enforces a spending cap by stopping resources.

source.title: Create and manage budgets

cards.statement: Excluding a resource group in Azure Advisor configuration also hides its recommendations from other users with access.
cards.explanation: Advisor configuration settings belong to the subscription or resource group, not to the viewer, so the same exclusion applies to everyone who has access to that scope.

source.title: Configure Azure Advisor recommendations view

cards.statement: Azure Storage firewall rules restrict Azure Resource Manager requests that change storage account settings.
cards.explanation: Storage firewall rules restrict data plane requests. Azure Resource Manager operations that manage the storage account remain outside those network restrictions.
cards.misconception: Storage network restrictions also block control plane management requests.

source.title: Guidelines and limitations for the Azure Storage firewall

cards.statement: A storage account virtual network rule can allow a subnet from another Azure subscription.
cards.explanation: Storage virtual network rules identify permitted subnets. The subnet and storage account may belong to different subscriptions.

source.title: Azure Storage firewall rules and network access control

cards.statement: An administrator can sign a user delegation SAS using a storage account access key.
cards.explanation: A user delegation SAS uses a user delegation key obtained with Microsoft Entra credentials, rather than a storage account access key.
cards.misconception: A user delegation SAS uses Shared Key signing like an account SAS.

source.title: Grant limited access to Azure Storage resources using shared access signatures

cards.statement: An account SAS can grant access to service-level operations such as reading storage service properties.
cards.explanation: An account SAS can delegate service-level operations as well as access to stored data. Service properties are an example of that broader operational scope.

source.title: Grant limited access to Azure Storage resources using shared access signatures

cards.statement: An account SAS can inherit its permissions and expiration from a stored access policy on a blob container.
cards.explanation: Stored access policies work with a service SAS. An account SAS specifies its access constraints in the SAS itself.
cards.misconception: Stored access policies apply to account SAS tokens as well as service SAS tokens.

source.title: Grant limited access to Azure Storage resources using shared access signatures

cards.statement: Azure Storage keeps a key-signed SAS valid until expiry when an administrator regenerates its signing key.
cards.explanation: Regenerating an access key revokes SAS tokens signed with that key. Clients using those tokens need newly generated SAS tokens.
cards.misconception: A SAS expiration time preserves a token after its signing key is regenerated.

source.title: Manage storage account access keys

cards.statement: An administrator chooses a different SMB identity source for individual shares within one storage account.
cards.explanation: A storage account uses one SMB identity source at a time, and that source applies to its Azure Files shares.
cards.misconception: SMB identity sources are configured independently at file share scope.

source.title: Overview of Azure Files identity-based authentication for SMB access

cards.statement: An SMB identity needs both share-level permission and file or directory permission for Azure Files access.
cards.explanation: Azure Files checks permissions at the share and at the file or directory. A share-level grant by itself does not grant access to the files inside.

source.title: Overview of Azure Files authorization and access control

cards.statement: Azure Files identity-based SMB access requires Kerberos in the account's SMB authentication settings.
cards.explanation: Kerberos is allowed by default in the SMB security settings. If a custom profile removes it, identity-based mounts fail, because Azure Files accepts NTLMv2 only with the storage account key.

source.title: SMB File Shares in Azure Files

cards.statement: Azure Files enforces file and directory ACLs when a client mounts SMB using the storage account key.
cards.explanation: Mounting an Azure file share with the storage account key grants immediate full access to its files and directories, regardless of their ACLs.
cards.misconception: File and directory ACLs limit clients that authenticate with a storage account key.

source.title: Configure directory and file-level permissions for Azure Files

cards.statement: Azure Storage keeps a Standard general-purpose v2 account's type fixed after an administrator creates it.
cards.explanation: To move data from a Standard general-purpose v2 account to a premium block blob account, create a replacement account and copy the data.

source.title: Overview of storage accounts

cards.statement: An administrator rehydrates or moves out an LRS account's archived blobs before converting the account to ZRS.
cards.explanation: ZRS, GZRS and RA-GZRS accounts don't support the archive tier, so archived blobs are rehydrated to an online tier or moved to an LRS, GRS or RA-GRS account before the conversion starts.

source.title: Change how a storage account is replicated

cards.statement: Azure Storage requires change feed on the source account before an administrator configures object replication.
cards.explanation: Azure Storage reads the source account's change feed to identify operations that object replication needs to copy.

source.title: Object replication for block blobs

cards.statement: An application can upload new blobs to an object replication destination container while its policy is active.
cards.explanation: While a replication policy is active, writes to its destination container fail with 409 (Conflict); reads and deletes still work. Remove the rule or policy before writing there.
cards.misconception: An object replication destination container accepts new uploads from client applications.

source.title: Object replication overview

cards.statement: Azure Storage copies a source blob's snapshots to its destination during object replication.
cards.explanation: Object replication excludes blob snapshots. Snapshots created for a source blob remain outside the replication policy's copied data.
cards.misconception: Object replication copies blob snapshots along with the blob's data.

source.title: Object replication for block blobs

cards.statement: An administrator who configures customer-managed keys at storage account creation uses a user-assigned managed identity.
cards.explanation: At account creation, Key Vault access for customer-managed keys uses a user-assigned managed identity; on an existing account either a user-assigned or a system-assigned identity works.

source.title: Customer-managed keys for account encryption

cards.statement: An administrator can resume an interrupted AzCopy transfer using the job's retained plan file.
cards.explanation: AzCopy uses its saved plan when resuming a failed or canceled job. It retries transfers in that plan that the job has yet to complete.

source.title: Find errors and resume jobs by using log and plan files in AzCopy

cards.statement: Azure Storage Explorer requires an Azure account sign-in before it attaches a blob container by its SAS URL.
cards.explanation: Storage Explorer attaches a blob container, file share, queue or table directly with its SAS URL. Signing in to Azure is a separate way to connect that lists subscriptions and their accounts.
cards.misconception: Attaching a resource by SAS URL in Storage Explorer depends on an Azure account sign-in.

source.title: Get started with Storage Explorer

cards.statement: By default, azcopy sync compares content hashes when deciding whether to update a matching blob.
cards.explanation: AzCopy sync normally compares file names and last modified timestamps. Content-hash comparison is an explicit option.
cards.misconception: AzCopy sync selects updated files by comparing their contents by default.
cards.volatilityNote: The default comparison behavior of the AzCopy sync command can change.

source.title: Synchronize with Azure Blob storage by using AzCopy

cards.statement: Administrators can edit a file inside an Azure Files share snapshot after creating the snapshot.
cards.explanation: Azure Files share snapshots preserve captured data as read-only. To change a captured file, copy it into a writable share first.
cards.misconception: A share snapshot acts as a writable copy of the file share.

source.title: Use Azure Files share snapshots

cards.statement: Azure Files can restore a deleted share's snapshots when an administrator undeletes that share.
cards.explanation: Undeleting a retained Azure file share restores its contents and the snapshots that existed when the share was deleted. The recovery operation brings the share back as a unit.

source.title: Azure file share soft delete

cards.statement: Azure Files converts an existing HDD file share to SSD (premium) when an administrator changes its media tier.
cards.explanation: Moving between Azure Files media tiers requires a new share on the target media tier and a data copy. An existing share's media tier stays fixed.
cards.misconception: A file share's media tier changes in place like a blob's access tier.

source.title: Plan an Azure Files deployment

cards.statement: An account's anonymous access restriction overrides a container's public setting on the Azure Blob Storage endpoint.
cards.explanation: For Blob service requests, an account's prohibition of anonymous access takes precedence over a container's public setting. The account setting closes anonymous access to such a container.

source.title: Remediate anonymous read access to blob data

cards.statement: Container soft delete recovers a blob an administrator deletes from a container that still exists.
cards.explanation: Container soft delete restores a deleted container and its contents. A blob deleted from an existing container needs blob-level protection, such as blob soft delete.
cards.misconception: Container soft delete protects individual deletions inside a surviving container.

source.title: Soft delete for containers

cards.statement: When an administrator updates a block blob's metadata with versioning enabled, Azure Storage creates a new blob version.
cards.explanation: Versioning treats Set Blob Metadata as a write: the current version becomes a previous version and a new current version records the change. Staging a block creates no version until commit.

source.title: Blob Versioning in Azure Storage

cards.statement: Administrators can enable blob versioning on storage accounts that use a hierarchical namespace.
cards.explanation: Azure Blob Storage currently excludes accounts with a hierarchical namespace from blob versioning. Administrators need another data-protection approach for those accounts.
cards.misconception: Hierarchical-namespace accounts offer the same blob versioning feature as flat-namespace accounts.
cards.volatilityNote: Hierarchical-namespace support for blob versioning may change.

source.title: Blob versioning

cards.statement: A new Azure Blob Storage lifecycle rule can act on existing blobs that match its filters and age conditions.
cards.explanation: Azure Storage evaluates stored objects against lifecycle rules during policy runs. Blobs that predate a new rule can qualify for its actions when their properties meet its conditions.

source.title: Lifecycle management performance characteristics

cards.statement: Administrators can select archive as the default access tier for a general-purpose v2 storage account.
cards.explanation: A storage account's default blob tier is an online tier. Administrators assign archive to individual eligible blobs rather than to the account's default access tier.
cards.misconception: The account's default access tier accepts archive just like an online tier.

source.title: Access tiers for blob data

cards.statement: Azure Storage automatically changes an archived source blob to hot when copying it into a new blob for rehydration.
cards.explanation: Copy-based rehydration creates a separate blob in the selected online tier. Azure Storage leaves the source blob unchanged in archive.
cards.misconception: Copy-based rehydration changes the source blob's tier along with the new destination blob.

source.title: Blob rehydration from the archive tier

cards.statement: An administrator can directly override an ARM template variable through the deployment's parameter file.
cards.explanation: A parameter file supplies values for parameters declared in the template. Variable values come from the template's definitions and expressions.
cards.misconception: A deployment parameter file directly overrides template variables as well as parameters.

source.title: Create an ARM template parameter file

cards.statement: Bicep automatically infers a dependency from a symbolic reference to another deployed resource's runtime property.
cards.explanation: A symbolic resource reference creates an implicit dependency in Bicep. Azure Resource Manager uses that dependency to deploy the referenced resource first.

source.title: Resource dependencies in Bicep

cards.statement: A Bicep module can deploy resources into a resource group different from its parent deployment's group.
cards.explanation: A module's explicit scope chooses its deployment target. An administrator sets that scope to the desired resource group when deploying from the parent Bicep file.

source.title: Bicep modules

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager masks a secure parameter's value inside an ordinary string deployment output.
cards.explanation: An ordinary string output exposes the secure parameter's value in deployment history. The parameter's secure type does not transfer protection to that output.
cards.misconception: A secure parameter keeps its value protected when an ordinary string output includes it.

source.title: Test cases for ARM templates: Outputs cannot include secrets

cards.statement: An incremental ARM deployment can reset omitted properties when Azure Resource Manager redeploys a resource.
cards.explanation: Incremental mode reapplies the resource configuration. An administrator includes intended nondefault properties to preserve them when redeploying the resource.

source.title: Azure Resource Manager deployment modes

cards.statement: What-if evaluates a utcNow() parameter default before comparing it with a resource's deployed tag value.
cards.explanation: What-if can't evaluate nondeterministic functions such as utcNow() or newGuid() outside a deployment, so it shows the expression as-is and can report a change.
cards.misconception: What-if resolves every template expression just as a real deployment does.

source.title: Bicep What-If: Preview Changes Before Deployment

cards.statement: For a parameter passed both inline and in a local parameter file, Azure Resource Manager uses the inline value.
cards.explanation: Inline values take precedence over the same parameter in a local parameter file. With an external parameter file URI, Resource Manager ignores inline values instead.

source.title: Create parameter file - Azure Resource Manager

cards.statement: An ARM template exported from a resource group preserves its original deployment's authored expressions.
cards.explanation: Resource-group export builds a new template from current resource settings. It does not recover the original template's parameter expressions.
cards.misconception: Exporting a resource group recovers the original authored deployment template.

source.title: Export a template from existing Azure resources

cards.statement: az bicep decompile can produce a Bicep file that needs repairs before an administrator deploys it.
cards.explanation: JSON-to-Bicep conversion uses a best-effort mapping. An administrator resolves warnings or errors in the generated file before relying on it for deployment.

source.title: Decompile an ARM template to Bicep

cards.statement: Encryption at host uses customer-managed keys for a VM's temporary disk when its managed disks use those keys.
cards.explanation: Encryption at host protects temporary disks with platform-managed keys. Choosing customer-managed keys for managed disks leaves the temporary disk's key source unchanged.
cards.misconception: Customer-managed key selection for managed disks also governs the VM's temporary disk.

source.title: Enable encryption at host for disks in the Azure portal

cards.statement: A successful resize of a running Azure VM preserves the guest operating system's uptime.
cards.explanation: Resizing a running Azure VM restarts the guest operating system. Schedule the size change for a time when the workload can tolerate that interruption.
cards.misconception: Resizing a running VM changes its compute capacity while keeping the guest running.

source.title: Change the size of a virtual machine

cards.statement: Azure continues to bill a managed data disk after an administrator detaches it from its VM.
cards.explanation: Detaching leaves the managed disk in place as an unattached disk that still incurs charges. Deleting the disk stops the charges and permanently removes its data.

source.title: Find and delete unattached Azure managed and unmanaged disks - Azure portal

cards.statement: Azure automatically formats a new empty managed data disk when an administrator attaches it to a Linux VM.
cards.explanation: Attaching an empty data disk makes it available to the Linux guest. The administrator then partitions and formats the disk before using it for file storage.
cards.misconception: Attaching a new managed data disk also prepares its guest file system.

source.title: Attach a data disk to a Linux VM using the Azure portal

cards.statement: Moving an Azure VM to another resource group changes the resource ID used by management scripts.
cards.explanation: A VM's resource ID includes its resource group. After moving the VM, update management references that still contain the old resource ID.

source.title: Move resources to a new resource group or subscription

cards.statement: An administrator can move an Azure VM between subscriptions belonging to different Microsoft Entra tenants.
cards.explanation: Azure Resource Manager requires the source and destination subscriptions to belong to the same Microsoft Entra tenant for a resource move.
cards.misconception: An ordinary subscription move transfers a VM across Microsoft Entra tenant boundaries.

source.title: Move resources to a new resource group or subscription

cards.statement: Azure Resource Mover deletes the source VM when an administrator commits a move to another Azure region.
cards.explanation: Committing a VM's region move leaves the source VM available for optional deletion. The administrator decides whether to remove that source resource.
cards.misconception: Committing a region move includes deleting the original VM.

source.title: Move Azure VMs across regions

cards.statement: Uniform scale set instances use the standard Azure VM APIs that administrators use for standalone VMs.
cards.explanation: Uniform orchestration uses scale-set-specific VM APIs to manage its instances. Standard standalone VM operations are a different API surface.
cards.misconception: Uniform scale set instances expose the same management API surface as standalone VMs.

source.title: Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure

cards.statement: Azure keeps a scale set's chosen orchestration mode fixed after an administrator creates the scale set.
cards.explanation: The orchestration mode is a creation-time choice. To use a different mode, create another scale set and move the workload.

source.title: Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Azure

cards.statement: Azure autoscale automatically combines a scale set's scale-out rule conditions using OR logic.
cards.explanation: A matching scale-out rule can trigger an increase in scale-set capacity. The configured capacity bounds and cooldown still govern the scaling action.

source.title: Understand autoscale settings

cards.statement: Azure Container Registry enables zone redundancy by default for a new Basic registry in a supported region.
cards.explanation: Supported regions give a Basic registry zone-redundant storage automatically. An administrator gets that protection when creating the registry.
cards.volatilityNote: Registry SKU packaging and the zone-redundancy creation default can change.

source.title: Azure Container Registry SKU features and limits

cards.statement: An administrator can restrict Azure Container Registry's admin account credentials to a chosen repository.
cards.explanation: The registry's admin credentials grant registry-wide push and pull access. Use an authentication method with repository-scoped permissions when access needs that restriction.
cards.misconception: The registry's admin account credentials can be scoped to a selected repository.

source.title: Azure Container Registry authentication options

cards.statement: Containers sharing an Azure Container Instances group can contact a peer container through localhost.
cards.explanation: An Azure Container Instances group shares a local network. Its containers communicate through localhost even on ports that the group does not publish externally.

source.title: Introduction to container groups

cards.statement: Azure Container Instances supports multiple Windows containers inside a single container group.
cards.explanation: Azure Container Instances restricts multi-container groups to Linux. A Windows container group runs a single container.
cards.misconception: Windows container groups offer the same multi-container deployment option as Linux groups.
cards.volatilityNote: Support for multi-container Windows groups may change.

source.title: What is Azure Container Instances?

cards.statement: After an administrator delegates a subnet to Azure Container Instances, that subnet holds container groups only.
cards.explanation: A delegated subnet serves container groups exclusively: deploying any other resource type to it fails, so administrators plan a dedicated subnet for Azure Container Instances.

source.title: Scenarios to use a virtual network with Azure Container Instances

cards.statement: Azure Container Instances can use a user-assigned managed identity for Azure Container Registry image pulls.
cards.explanation: Assign the user-assigned identity to the container group and grant it image-pull access on the registry. Select that identity for the group's registry authentication.

source.title: Deploy to Azure Container Instances from Azure Container Registry using a managed identity

cards.statement: Azure Container Apps can increase a running replica's CPU allocation automatically as application load grows.
cards.explanation: Container Apps autoscaling changes replica counts. CPU and memory allocations come from the revision's container settings.
cards.misconception: Azure Container Apps automatically resizes the CPU allocation of a running replica.
cards.volatilityNote: Azure Container Apps may add vertical autoscaling support.

source.title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

cards.statement: An Azure Container Apps queue scale rule applies its message threshold per replica when calculating replica demand.
cards.explanation: The queue rule's target message count represents demand per replica. Container Apps compares queue demand with that target to calculate the desired replica count.

source.title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

cards.statement: An ingress-disabled Azure Container Apps app using default scaling settings restarts automatically from zero.
cards.explanation: Azure Container Apps' default HTTP rule has no trigger when ingress is disabled. After scale-to-zero, that rule leaves the app idle instead of restarting it.
cards.misconception: The default scale rule restarts a background app from zero replicas even when ingress is disabled.
cards.volatilityNote: The default scale rule and its zero-replica behavior can change.

source.title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

cards.statement: Azure Container Apps routes traffic to a new revision in single revision mode before readiness checks pass.
cards.explanation: With ingress enabled, single revision mode keeps traffic on the existing revision until the new revision is ready. An update that fails readiness leaves traffic with the existing revision.
cards.misconception: Single revision mode directs traffic to a newly deployed revision before that revision passes readiness checks.

source.title: Update and deploy changes in Azure Container Apps

cards.statement: With per-app scaling disabled, an App Service staging slot shares worker resources with its production app.
cards.explanation: Deployment slots run on the App Service plan's workers. With per-app scaling disabled, staging activity consumes compute resources that also serve the production app.

source.title: Azure App Service plans

cards.statement: App Service keeps a slot's managed identity attached to that slot when an administrator swaps app content.
cards.explanation: A slot swap moves app content while the managed identity stays with its original slot. Check the identity permissions of the destination slot before moving content into it.

source.title: Set up staging environments in Azure App Service

cards.statement: An App Service app keeps its current process running when an administrator changes an app setting.
cards.explanation: Changing an App Service app setting triggers an app restart. The restarted app receives the updated setting in its startup environment.
cards.misconception: Editing an app setting updates configuration while preserving the app's existing process.

source.title: Configure an App Service app

cards.statement: App Service supports auto swap for Linux apps when their staging slot finishes warming up.
cards.explanation: Auto swap is unsupported for App Service apps on Linux. An administrator uses an explicit slot swap to promote a staged Linux deployment.
cards.misconception: Auto swap works for Linux apps once the staging slot passes warm-up.

source.title: Set up staging environments in Azure App Service

cards.statement: An administrator can validate an App Service custom domain by TXT record while traffic still goes to an external site.
cards.explanation: A TXT record containing the App Service domain verification ID proves ownership before the administrator redirects the domain's traffic records to the new app.

source.title: Migrate an existing domain to Azure App Service

cards.statement: App Service issues its free managed certificate for a wildcard domain after domain validation succeeds.
cards.explanation: The free App Service managed certificate excludes wildcard domains. To secure a wildcard custom domain, an administrator supplies a suitable certificate through another supported method.
cards.misconception: A verified wildcard custom domain qualifies for the free App Service managed certificate.
cards.volatilityNote: The free App Service managed certificate's supported domain patterns may change.

source.title: Add and manage TLS/SSL certificates in Azure App Service

cards.statement: An administrator can directly set separate minimum TLS versions for an App Service app and its SCM site.
cards.explanation: App Service gives the main app endpoint and the SCM deployment endpoint independent minimum TLS settings. Configure both endpoints to meet the intended connection requirements.

source.title: Manage minimum TLS versions for Azure App Service, Azure Functions, and Logic Apps (Standard)

cards.statement: App Service virtual network integration allows clients to connect directly to an app through its private address.
cards.explanation: App Service virtual network integration routes outbound calls from an app into a virtual network. Use a private endpoint when clients need private inbound access to the app.
cards.misconception: Virtual network integration gives the app a private inbound endpoint for clients.

source.title: Integrate your app with an Azure virtual network

cards.statement: An administrator can authorize App Service custom backups with the app's managed identity on the storage account.
cards.explanation: App Service custom backup and restore operations use SAS authorization for their storage account. Assigning storage permissions to the app's managed identity does not replace that SAS requirement.
cards.misconception: A managed identity with storage permissions replaces SAS authorization for App Service custom backups.

source.title: Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service

cards.statement: An administrator configures App Service automatic backups to run on a schedule chosen for the app.
cards.explanation: App Service controls the automatic backup schedule. An administrator uses custom backups when the application needs administrator-selected backup timing.
cards.misconception: The administrator chooses the schedule of the platform's automatic backups.

source.title: Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service

cards.statement: Azure autoscale can change an App Service plan's capacity range through a scheduled profile.
cards.explanation: Schedule-based Azure autoscale applies to the App Service plan. An administrator defines profiles for anticipated demand at particular times.

source.title: Get started with autoscale in Azure

cards.statement: Azure refreshes a peer's routes for newly added address space before an administrator syncs the peering.
cards.explanation: After changing a peered virtual network's address space, synchronize its peers. That synchronization updates the peering with the changed address ranges.
cards.misconception: Resizing a peered virtual network updates its peers' address-space information before synchronization.

source.title: Azure virtual network peering

cards.statement: Azure routes traffic between networks A and C through B when A peers with B and B peers with C.
cards.explanation: The A-B and B-C peerings provide separate routes. Communication between A and C needs another connection or an explicitly configured forwarding path.
cards.misconception: Virtual network peering creates a direct relationship across a chain of existing peerings.

source.title: Create, change, or delete virtual network peering

cards.statement: An administrator can enable gateway transit between virtual networks peered across Azure regions.
cards.explanation: Global virtual network peering supports gateway transit. Configure the peering settings to let a network use the gateway hosted in its peer's region.

source.title: Azure virtual network peering

cards.statement: A virtual network using a peer's remote gateway can also use its own gateway for on-premises connectivity.
cards.explanation: A virtual network using a remote gateway excludes a gateway of its own. Choose a local gateway or configure the network to use its peer's gateway.
cards.misconception: A network combines its own gateway with a remote gateway supplied through peering.

source.title: Azure virtual network peering

cards.statement: Azure retains a VM's Standard public IP address when an administrator stops and deallocates the VM.
cards.explanation: Standard public IPs use static allocation. Deallocating the VM leaves its public IP resource and assigned address in place.

source.title: Public IP addresses

cards.statement: With a 0.0.0.0/0 user-defined route to an appliance, Azure sends traffic between a virtual network's subnets through it.
cards.explanation: Azure uses longest prefix match: the system route for the virtual network's address space is more specific than 0.0.0.0/0, so traffic between subnets stays local unless a route names that prefix.
cards.misconception: A default 0.0.0.0/0 user-defined route captures traffic between subnets of the same virtual network.

source.title: Azure virtual network traffic routing

cards.statement: For routes with the same matching prefix, Azure chooses a user-defined route ahead of a BGP route.
cards.explanation: When matching prefixes are equal, Azure ranks a user-defined route ahead of one learned through BGP. This lets an administrator override that advertised path.

source.title: Azure virtual network traffic routing

cards.statement: Azure requires IP forwarding on a virtual appliance's network interface to carry traffic for other destinations.
cards.explanation: The Azure NIC's forwarding setting disables address checks that would reject transit packets. Configure the appliance's guest networking separately to handle those packets.

source.title: Azure virtual network traffic routing

cards.statement: An administrator directly obtains a VM NIC's effective routes by listing its subnet's user-defined routes.
cards.explanation: Inspect effective routes on the VM's network interface to see the combined routing information. Listing the subnet's user-defined routes omits other route sources.
cards.misconception: The subnet's user-defined route list is the VM network interface's complete effective route list.

source.title: Create, change, or delete a route table

cards.statement: An administrator associates an Azure route table with subnets across virtual networks in its subscription and region.
cards.explanation: A route table can serve subnets in multiple virtual networks within its subscription and region. Associate it with the subnets that need the shared custom routes.

source.title: Create, change, or delete a route table

cards.statement: For overlapping NSG rules, Azure processes the rule with the lower priority number first.
cards.explanation: Lower priority numbers give an NSG rule precedence over higher numbers. An administrator uses that ordering to decide which matching rule controls a connection.

source.title: Create, change, or delete a network security group

cards.statement: For inbound traffic, Azure evaluates a VM's network interface NSG before the NSG associated with its subnet.
cards.explanation: Azure checks a subnet's NSG before the network interface's NSG for inbound traffic. An administrator tracing an inbound connection starts with the subnet rules.
cards.misconception: Inbound NSG evaluation starts at the VM's network interface.

source.title: How network security groups filter network traffic

cards.statement: Azure closes an established TCP connection when an administrator removes its NSG allow rule.
cards.explanation: Removing an NSG allow rule leaves an established connection running. Azure applies the changed rules to new connection attempts, so test with a fresh connection.
cards.misconception: Deleting an NSG allow rule immediately disconnects sessions that used it.

source.title: Azure network security groups overview

cards.statement: Azure accepts a network interface into an application security group only from the first member's virtual network.
cards.explanation: The first network interface added establishes an application security group's virtual network. Subsequent member interfaces belong to that same network.

source.title: Application security groups

cards.statement: An administrator can combine several service tags in the destination field of a single NSG security rule.
cards.explanation: An NSG rule's destination field accepts a service tag rather than a list of tags. Use separate rules when different service tags need matching.
cards.misconception: Augmented NSG rules accept lists of service tags in the same way as lists of explicit IP addresses.
cards.volatilityNote: The restriction on combining service tags in an NSG rule may change.

source.title: Azure network security groups overview

cards.statement: A new Azure Bastion Standard deployment requires AzureBastionSubnet to have a /26 or larger address range.
cards.explanation: A new Standard Bastion host needs a dedicated AzureBastionSubnet with at least a /26 address range. An administrator reserves sufficient subnet space before deploying the host.
cards.volatilityNote: The fixed /26 minimum subnet requirement can change.

source.title: About Azure Bastion configuration settings

cards.statement: With an Azure Storage service endpoint on its subnet, a VM calls same-region storage accounts from its private IP.
cards.explanation: A storage service endpoint switches the subnet's traffic to same-region accounts from public to private IPv4 sources, so firewall rules listing the VMs' public IPs stop matching.

source.title: Azure virtual network service endpoints

cards.statement: Azure Storage's public DNS records can return a private endpoint's IP for the default Blob hostname.
cards.explanation: The public DNS records for Azure Storage lead to the service's public address. Private-endpoint clients need DNS resolution that supplies the endpoint's private address.
cards.misconception: Azure's published public DNS records expose the storage private endpoint's private IP address.

source.title: Use private endpoints for Azure Storage

cards.statement: Azure sets public network access to Disabled when an administrator adds a storage private endpoint.
cards.explanation: Azure Storage keeps public endpoint access under separate control. An administrator restricts or disables that public access independently of creating a private endpoint.
cards.misconception: Creating a private endpoint also disables the storage account's public endpoint.

source.title: Use private endpoints for Azure Storage

cards.statement: Azure DNS automatically delegates a purchased domain when an administrator creates its matching public zone.
cards.explanation: The domain owner updates the registrar's name-server delegation to the servers assigned to the Azure DNS zone. Creating the zone leaves this registrar task for the owner.
cards.misconception: Creating a public Azure DNS zone also updates the domain registrar's delegation.

source.title: Tutorial: Host your domain in Azure DNS

cards.statement: Azure Private DNS can autoregister a VM's secondary network interface in a linked private DNS zone.
cards.explanation: Azure Private DNS creates automatic VM records for the primary network interface. An administrator creates records manually for a VM's additional network interfaces.
cards.misconception: Autoregistration discovers and registers a VM's secondary network interfaces.

source.title: What is the autoregistration feature in Azure DNS private zones?

cards.statement: A VM using Azure-provided DNS can resolve records in a linked private zone with autoregistration disabled.
cards.explanation: A resolution link makes a private zone's existing records available to Azure-provided DNS clients in the linked network. Enabling VM record registration is a separate choice.

source.title: What is a virtual network link?

cards.statement: Azure DNS automatically empties an alias record set when an administrator deletes its Standard public IP target.
cards.explanation: Deleting an alias record's Standard public IP target leaves an empty record set in Azure DNS. This clears the dangling reference while retaining the record-set resource.

source.title: Azure DNS alias records overview

cards.statement: By default, VMs using custom DNS servers bypass those servers to query a linked Azure private DNS zone.
cards.explanation: VM queries go to their configured custom DNS servers first. The administrator configures those servers to forward the Azure private namespace to a resolver that can reach the linked zone.
cards.misconception: A linked Azure private DNS zone makes a VM bypass its configured custom DNS servers.

source.title: Troubleshoot DNS resolution failures caused by conditional forwarder misconfiguration in Azure

cards.statement: A regional Standard Load Balancer's backend pool holds VMs from a single virtual network.
cards.explanation: A Standard Load Balancer's VM backend pool stays within a single virtual network. Its backend VMs may occupy different subnets in that network.

source.title: Azure Load Balancer SKUs

cards.statement: Standard Load Balancer keeps an established TCP mapping when its backend fails a probe and other backends stay healthy.
cards.explanation: A backend's failed probe changes selection for new flows. Standard Load Balancer leaves existing TCP flows on that backend until connection closure or idle timeout.

source.title: Azure Load Balancer health probes

cards.statement: Standard Load Balancer can map different frontend IPs to the same VM IP and TCP port with Floating IP disabled.
cards.explanation: Enable Floating IP on rules that send traffic from different frontends to the same backend IP and TCP port. Floating IP preserves the frontend address as the packet's destination.
cards.misconception: Different frontend IPs can share the same backend IP and TCP port with Floating IP disabled.

source.title: Multiple frontends for Azure Load Balancer

cards.statement: An inbound NAT rule can distribute traffic for a mapped frontend port among several healthy backend VMs.
cards.explanation: An inbound NAT rule maps a frontend port to a designated backend VM and port. Traffic for that mapping reaches its selected VM rather than being balanced across the pool.
cards.misconception: An inbound NAT rule balances a mapped frontend port's traffic across healthy backend VMs.

source.title: Inbound NAT rules

cards.statement: An administrator can set an internal Standard Load Balancer's frontend to a chosen unused address in its subnet.
cards.explanation: Set the internal frontend's allocation to Static and select an available address from its subnet. This gives clients a stable private destination for the load balancer.

source.title: Azure Load Balancer portal settings

cards.statement: Azure Monitor freezes a diagnostic category group's collected categories when an administrator creates the setting.
cards.explanation: When Microsoft changes a diagnostic category group's membership, Azure Monitor updates collection to match. Selecting a group keeps the setting aligned with that group's categories.
cards.misconception: A diagnostic category group captures a fixed list of categories at the time the setting is created.

source.title: Diagnostic settings in Azure Monitor

cards.statement: A Log Analytics query can combine data from workspaces in different Azure subscriptions.
cards.explanation: A cross-workspace query retrieves data from explicitly referenced workspaces, including those in other subscriptions. The administrator needs query access to the referenced data.

source.title: Query data across Log Analytics workspaces, applications, and resources in Azure Monitor

cards.statement: An alert processing rule can suppress notifications for resources in another Azure subscription.
cards.explanation: An alert processing rule applies to resources within its own subscription. Create a separate rule in another subscription to process that subscription's alerts.
cards.misconception: An alert processing rule's scope extends to resources in other subscriptions.

source.title: Alert processing rules for Azure Monitor alerts

cards.statement: An alert processing rule that adds action groups overrides a matching rule that suppresses action groups.
cards.explanation: A suppression rule takes precedence when addition and suppression rules match the same fired alert. Azure Monitor suppresses the alert's action groups.
cards.misconception: An action-group addition rule wins when it conflicts with a suppression rule.

source.title: Alert processing rules for Azure Monitor alerts

cards.statement: Azure Monitor runs an alert rule's attached action groups in the order the administrator adds them.
cards.explanation: Azure Monitor invokes an alert rule's action groups concurrently. Their attachment order does not establish an execution sequence for notifications or automated actions.
cards.misconception: An alert rule's action groups execute sequentially in their attachment order.

source.title: Create and manage action groups in Azure Monitor

cards.statement: A VM's data collection rule can filter Windows Application events by severity before Azure Monitor Agent sends them.
cards.explanation: In the rule's Windows events data source, choose the Application log and the desired severities. Azure Monitor Agent collects matching events for the associated VM.

source.title: Collect Windows events from virtual machines with Azure Monitor Agent

cards.statement: Storage insights shows a storage account's capacity and latency from metrics that Azure collects by default.
cards.explanation: Storage insights needs nothing enabled or configured: it reads the storage metrics Azure collects by default, so an administrator creates no diagnostic setting to use it.

source.title: Monitor Azure Storage services with Azure Monitor Storage insights

cards.statement: Network insights topology includes connected Azure resources across multiple resource groups in the same view.
cards.explanation: Network insights topology represents resource relationships across resource groups. An administrator can follow a network connection beyond a resource group's organizational boundary.

source.title: Network insights

cards.statement: An Access allowed result from IP flow verify confirms the VM's application is listening on the tested port.
cards.explanation: Access allowed describes the security-rule evaluation for the supplied packet. IP flow verify evaluates rules rather than checking whether the application accepts a connection.
cards.misconception: A permitted security-rule result proves that the application is listening on the requested port.

source.title: IP flow verify overview

cards.statement: Connection monitor can use an Azure VM's installed Azure Monitor Agent to run connectivity probes from that source.
cards.explanation: Connection monitor runs Azure VM source checks through the Network Watcher Agent virtual machine extension. Install that extension on an Azure VM used as a monitoring source.
cards.misconception: An Azure VM source uses Azure Monitor Agent to run Connection monitor probes.
tags: Network Watcher Agent virtual machine extension

source.title: Connection monitor overview

cards.statement: Administrators configure Azure Disk Backup in a Recovery Services vault to protect a managed disk.
cards.explanation: Configure Azure Disk Backup in a Backup vault. The managed disk's backup instance and policy belong to that vault.
cards.misconception: Azure Disk Backup uses the same vault type as whole-VM backup.

source.title: Overview of Azure Disk Backup

cards.statement: An administrator can use a Recovery Services vault in one Azure region to back up an Azure VM in another region.
cards.explanation: For Azure VM backup, the Recovery Services vault belongs in the VM's region. Deploy a vault in the workload's region when configuring protection.
cards.misconception: A Recovery Services vault can centrally back up Azure VMs located in other regions.

source.title: Create and configure a Recovery Services vault

cards.statement: Azure Backup freezes a Recovery Services vault's redundancy setting when an administrator configures backup.
cards.explanation: Choose the vault's storage redundancy before enabling VM protection. Azure Backup disables changes to that setting once a backup is configured.

source.title: Create and configure a Recovery Services vault

cards.statement: An administrator can change a protected VM from an Enhanced backup policy to a Standard backup policy.
cards.explanation: Azure Backup prevents changing a protected VM's policy type from Enhanced to Standard. Plan for that restriction when selecting an Enhanced policy.
cards.misconception: A VM protected by an Enhanced policy can return to a Standard policy through a policy change.

source.title: Back up an Azure VM by using the Enhanced policy

cards.statement: Azure Backup can remove later-added data disks from a VM's attachments during a Replace existing restore.
cards.explanation: A Replace existing restore applies the disk configuration captured in the recovery point. Data disks attached later fall outside that restored configuration.

source.title: How to restore Azure VM data in Azure portal

cards.statement: An administrator sends vault diagnostic data to Log Analytics to populate Azure Backup reports.
cards.explanation: Azure Backup reports read their reporting data from Log Analytics workspaces. Configure the vault's diagnostic settings to send the relevant data to a workspace.

source.title: Configure Azure Backup reports

cards.statement: By default, Azure Backup generates a built-in Azure Monitor alert when a scheduled VM backup succeeds.
cards.explanation: Azure Backup's built-in job alerts flag failures rather than routine successes. A successful VM backup appears in its job status.
cards.misconception: Azure Backup's built-in alerts include routine notifications for successful scheduled backups.
cards.volatilityNote: The default built-in alert categories for Azure VM backup jobs can change.

source.title: Monitoring and Reporting solutions for Azure Backup

cards.statement: Azure Site Recovery requires its cache storage account in the target region for Azure-to-Azure replication.
cards.explanation: The Site Recovery cache storage account belongs in the source region. VM disk changes pass through that cache before Site Recovery sends them to target storage.
cards.misconception: Site Recovery stages replication data in a cache account located in the target region.

source.title: Azure to Azure disaster recovery architecture

cards.statement: Azure Site Recovery continues Azure-to-Azure replication while an administrator runs a VM test failover.
cards.explanation: A Site Recovery test failover creates a test VM from replicated data. Production replication continues during the drill.

source.title: Run a test failover (disaster recovery drill) to Azure

cards.statement: An administrator reprotects a failed-over VM with Azure Site Recovery before failing it back to its primary region.
cards.explanation: After committing failover, reprotect the VM to start replication from the secondary region toward the primary region. Fail back after reprotection completes.

source.title: Reprotect failed over Azure virtual machines to the primary region
